Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Police in Boston, Massachusetts, are searching for a man suspected in the murder of one woman and the armed robbery of two others, all of whom, they say, he may have met through their Craigslist ads for personal services. Julissa Brisman, 26, was described as "a really sweet, goofy, energetic kid." Officers discovered New York resident Julissa Brisman, 26, unconscious with multiple gunshot wounds at Boston's Copley Marriott Hotel on Tuesday night. She was transferred to Boston Medical Center, where she died shortly afterward. Police said Brisman, a model, offered massages via Craigslist, a popular online classified ad service. The confrontation between Brisman and her killer seems to have begun as an attempted robbery, police said. "It appears that there was a struggle between the victim and the suspect in the threshold of the hotel room immediately prior to the shooting," the Boston Police Department said in a statement on its Web site. Police speculate the man may also be responsible for the recent robberies of two other young women who offered personal services via Craigslist. Four days before Brisman's slaying, a 29-year-old woman was robbed at gunpoint at a Westin Hotel in Boston. Police spokesman Joe Zanola would not disclose the details of her Craigslist ad but said she and Brisman were "involved in similar professions." On Thursday night at a Holiday Inn Express in Warwick, Rhode Island, a man tied up and demanded money from a 26-year-old dancer who had posted a Craigslist advertisement, according to Warwick's police chief, Col. Stephen McCartney. The robbery was interrupted when the woman's husband entered the room. After pointing his gun at the husband, the suspect fled, according to McCartney. He said that no conclusions could be made but allowed that the incident "may be related to similar crimes occurring in the Boston area." Matthew Terhune, a photographer who met Brisman when he took pictures of her for a calendar last year, described her as "just a really sweet, goofy, energetic kid." He added that she was enrolled in Alcoholics Anonymous and was contemplating counseling fellow recovering addicts. He had been unaware of her side job as an Internet masseuse. Surveillance videos from the hotel where Brisman was murdered showed a tall, clean-cut young blond man in a black windbreaker leaving the property, said the Boston Police Department, which is asking the public's help in identifying the man. Representatives from Craigslist did not respond to a request for comment.

The robbery was interrupted when the woman’s husband entered the room. After pointing his gun at the husband, the suspect fled, McCartney said. Although he cautioned that no conclusions could be drawn, he acknowledged that the incident “may be related to similar crimes occurring in the Boston area.”

Matthew Terhune, a photographer who met Brisman when he photographed her for a calendar the previous year, described her as “just a really sweet, goofy, energetic kid.” He added that she was enrolled in Alcoholics Anonymous and was considering counseling fellow recovering addicts. ## Digital Trail and Hotel Cameras Led Police to Suspect in 2009 “Craigslist Killer” Case

**BOSTON —** The investigation began with a fatal shooting inside a luxury hotel near Copley Square and quickly widened into a regional search for a young, clean-cut gunman believed to be targeting women who advertised personal services on Craigslist.

Within six days of the killing of 25-year-old Julissa Brisman at the Boston Marriott Copley Place in April 2009, police had arrested Philip Markoff, a 23-year-old Boston University medical student. Investigators said hotel surveillance recordings, witness accounts and electronic records associated with online advertisements and cellular telephones connected Markoff to Brisman’s death and two similar attacks.

Markoff pleaded not guilty and died by suicide in jail in August 2010, before the charges could be tried. As a result, the evidence against him was never tested in a full criminal trial.

### Shooting at the Copley Marriott

Brisman, a New York-area woman who advertised massage services on Craigslist, arranged to meet a customer at the Boston Marriott Copley Place on April 14, 2009.

Authorities said the encounter turned violent at the entrance to her room. Prosecutors alleged that the attacker tried to restrain and rob Brisman, striking her and shooting her several times when she resisted. Hotel guests reported hearing a disturbance, and Brisman was found gravely wounded near the doorway. She was taken to Boston Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead.

The location complicated the initial investigation. The Marriott is part of the busy Copley Place complex, an area filled with hotel guests, shoppers, office workers and visitors moving through interconnected buildings and nearby streets. Detectives began reviewing security recordings and interviewing people who had been in the hotel.

The surveillance system had not recorded the shooting inside the room. Instead, cameras captured a man moving through public areas of the property around the time of the killing. Images showed a tall, young white man with short blond or light-colored hair, dressed neatly and carrying himself in a manner witnesses described as unremarkable or “clean-cut.”

Police released surveillance images to the public, hoping someone would recognize him. The photographs and video became central to the highly publicized search.

### Similar robbery days earlier

Detectives soon compared the Marriott killing with an April 10 robbery at the nearby Westin Copley Place.

In that case, a woman who had advertised escort services online told police that a man entered her hotel room, displayed a handgun, restrained her with plastic ties and stole cash and other property. She survived and was able to give investigators a description.

Her account closely resembled the emerging profile of the man seen in the Marriott footage: a white male in his 20s, about 6 feet tall or taller, with light hair and a clean-cut appearance. Police also examined recordings from the Westin and the surrounding Copley Square hotel complex.

The use of online advertisements, the hotel setting, the apparent intention to rob the women and the method of restraint led investigators to consider whether the crimes had been committed by the same person.

### Rhode Island attack broadens the search

A third incident on April 16 further strengthened that theory.

A woman who had advertised dancing or escort services online arranged to meet a customer at a Holiday Inn Express in Warwick, Rhode Island. She told police that the man pulled a gun and attempted to restrain and rob her. The encounter was interrupted when her husband entered the room, and the assailant fled.

Once again, the reported attacker was described as young, tall, white and blond or light-haired. Investigators in Massachusetts and Rhode Island began sharing witness statements, hotel records and surveillance recordings.

The Rhode Island footage was particularly important because it offered another view of a man whose appearance and clothing were consistent with the person recorded in Boston. Though the images were not always sharp enough for an immediate identification, police could compare the suspect’s build, face, hair, movements and clothing across multiple locations.

### Online records provide a lead

The case became an early and prominent example of police using digital evidence from online classified advertisements.

Investigators obtained records connected with the Craigslist postings and communications used to arrange the appointments. They also examined telephone records associated with the contacts. Authorities said the electronic trail led them to Markoff, who lived in Quincy and was studying medicine at Boston University.

Police placed him under surveillance. On April 20, officers stopped Markoff on Interstate 95 in Walpole as he traveled with his fiancée toward Connecticut. He was taken into custody without a public confrontation.

At the time, Markoff did not resemble the stereotype many people associated with a serial robber. He was a medical student, was engaged to be married and had no widely known history of violent crime. His arrest intensified national interest in the case.

### Searches and physical evidence

After the arrest, investigators searched Markoff’s apartment and vehicle. Prosecutors later said they recovered a semiautomatic handgun, ammunition, plastic restraints and other items they considered relevant to the hotel attacks. Authorities also reported finding property they believed was linked to the victims.

Forensic testing and firearms analysis became part of the prosecution’s case. Police alleged that the weapon recovered after Markoff’s arrest was connected to the bullets used to kill Brisman.

Investigators also assembled a timeline using hotel surveillance video, computer and telephone data, witness identifications and evidence collected during the searches. Prosecutors argued that the three incidents showed a common pattern: women advertising services online were contacted, met in hotels and confronted by an armed robber who attempted to bind them.

### Charges and unresolved trial

Markoff was charged in Massachusetts with Brisman’s murder, armed robbery, kidnapping and other offenses related to the Boston cases. He was also accused in connection with the Rhode Island attack. He pleaded not guilty.

From the beginning, his defense emphasized that an arrest and indictment were not proof of guilt and that the government’s evidence would need to be challenged in court. Markoff remained in custody while the case moved toward trial.

That trial never took place. On Aug. 15, 2010, Markoff was found dead in his cell at Boston’s Nashua Street Jail. Authorities ruled his death a suicide.

Because Markoff died before trial, no jury determined whether prosecutors had proved the allegations beyond a reasonable doubt. The charges were never resolved by a verdict.

The investigation nevertheless became nationally known as the “Craigslist killer” case, a label popularized by news organizations rather than law enforcement. It drew attention both to the dangers faced by people meeting customers through online advertisements and to the growing importance of electronic records and ubiquitous security cameras in criminal investigations.

For Boston detectives, the case turned on the convergence of traditional and digital police work: survivors who supplied consistent descriptions, hotel employees and guests who helped establish a timeline, cameras that recorded the suspect’s movements, and online and telephone records that led investigators from an anonymous advertisement to a specific individual.
